newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australian dlr simmers down after furious run.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australian dlr simmers down after furious run.

text.p: The Australian dollar cooled a little Wednesday as its recent blazing rally drew profit-taking.

The currency stepped back almost 1/2 cent from Tuesday's two-month US$0.7912 high and analysts cautioned it was still overbought on technical indicators so a lapse to US$0.7845 would be no surprise. Nevertheless, sentiment was reportedly bullish and most expected a renewed rise as long as US$0.7820 held.

Domestic data on December quarter GDP proved an anti-climax as growth came in much as expected at 0.5 percent and the market was preoccupied with the outlook for this year which was already bright enough to eclipse all thought of another rate cut.
By 5.00 pm (0600 GMT) the dollar was parked at US$0.7870/75 after orbiting in a US$0.7865/86 range for the session having drifted back from US$0.7905/10 late here Tuesday.
Dealers thought the retracement modest given the currency had climbed from US$0.7750 on Friday and a low of US$0.7550 less than a month ago.

Most looked for a bout of consolidation in a US$0.7820/7920 band before favourable fundamentals, both here and abroad, lifted it toward the next bull target of US$0.7960. The loss of US$0.7740 at any time would reverse the uptrend, they added.
On the crosses, the dollar actually added to recent gains.
It nudged up to 1.3484/3500 marks and 1.1695/10 francs from 1.3422/35 and 1.1671/86 late Tuesday as funds continued to exit low yielding currencies across the world.
The attraction of the dollar's relatively high interest rate was also augmented by rumbling concerns the timetable for European Monetary Union might vulnerable to slippage.
The dollar did ease off on the yen to 95.77/87 from 96.34/44 late Tuesday, but again this was a respectable performance given it touched a 4-1/2 year high of 96.50 yesterday.
In trade weighted terms the profit-taking pared the index to 60.4 from Tuesday's five year high of 60.6.
The currency had an uncomfortable moment after reports circulated Treasurer Peter Costello, at a press conference on the GDP data, had said the dollar was too high.

In fact what he said was the currency was "quite high" and "pretty strong" and once this became clear the market quickly steadied. The government always stresses that it has no preffered target rate for the dollar, although Costello did note that the current strength was a pressure on exporters.
Costello, like the market, treated the GDP data as an historical footenote for 1996 and concentrated on the improving outlook for 1997 following a run of more up-to-date figures.

The average measure of GDP rose a much as expected 0.5 percent in the quarter, but annual growth was a slower than forecast 3.1 percent due to downward revisions in some prior quarters. Growth would have been 3.5 percent otherwise.
Growth was led by private consumption and equipment investment while imports were a big detractor.

The inflation measures remained subdued with the expenditure based GDP deflator rising 0.4 percent on the quarter and 1.7 percent on the year. The September quarter performance was not as impressive as originally reported, however, as the initial 0.4 percent fall was revised to a 0.1 percent rise.
Far more important for the outlook for monetary policy, and thus markets, would be next week's helping of indicators.
These included employment and job advertisements for February, housing finance and private sector credit for January and consumer sentiment for March.

If these maintained the strengthening trend seen in other recent figures the risk of another easing would fade yet further into the background, perhaps even leaving room for thoughts of a tightening down the track.
